title: Yaa and the Mystery of Changing Life

pages.text: Inside the science museum in Accra, twelve-year-old Yaa leaned over a glass case containing dark stone slabs. Pressed into the rock were the outlines of ancient fish and fern leaves that looked different from any living species she had ever seen. ‘Madam Abena,’ Yaa asked, ‘why do these fossils look partly familiar and partly strange?’
sentences: Inside the science museum in Accra, twelve-year-old Yaa leaned over a glass case containing dark stone slabs.
Pressed into the rock were the outlines of ancient fish and fern leaves that looked different from any living species she had ever seen.
‘Madam Abena,’ Yaa asked, ‘why do these fossils look partly familiar and partly strange?’
pages.alt: Yaa and Kwame examine stone fossils of ancient fish and ferns in a glass museum case with Madam Abena.

pages.text: Madam Abena adjusted her spectacles and smiled. ‘Because life on Earth has not stayed frozen in time, Yaa. Those fossils are preserved remains and traces left in rock layers over millions of years. Deeper rock layers hold older fossils, and higher layers hold younger ones, giving us a timeline of how living things have changed.’
sentences: Madam Abena adjusted her spectacles and smiled.
‘Because life on Earth has not stayed frozen in time, Yaa.
Those fossils are preserved remains and traces left in rock layers over millions of years.
Deeper rock layers hold older fossils, and higher layers hold younger ones, giving us a timeline of how living things have changed.’
pages.alt: Madam Abena points to a colourful wall diagram of layered rock cliffs with older fossils at the bottom and newer fossils near the top.

pages.text: At the next table, Yaa looked at a tray of mounted savannah grass beetles collected decades apart. Even within a single family of beetles, no two were identical: some had slightly darker brown shells, and others had paler tan shells. ‘This is inherited variation,’ said Madam Abena. ‘Offspring inherit traits from their parents through DNA, with natural differences from one individual to another.’
sentences: At the next table, Yaa looked at a tray of mounted savannah grass beetles collected decades apart.
Even within a single family of beetles, no two were identical: some had slightly darker brown shells, and others had paler tan shells.
‘This is inherited variation,’ said Madam Abena.
‘Offspring inherit traits from their parents through DNA, with natural differences from one individual to another.’
pages.alt: Yaa looks through a magnifying glass at a museum tray of brown and tan beetles of slightly different shades.

pages.text: Kwame frowned thoughtfully. ‘So if the dry bush turns dark brown after a bushfire, do the pale beetles decide to turn dark brown so birds cannot spot them?’
sentences: Kwame frowned thoughtfully.
‘So if the dry bush turns dark brown after a bushfire, do the pale beetles decide to turn dark brown so birds cannot spot them?’
pages.alt: Kwame points at the pale tan beetles with a puzzled expression as he asks his question.

pages.text: ‘No, Kwame, and that is a crucial point,’ said Madam Abena. ‘An individual organism cannot evolve or change its inherited colour simply because it needs or wishes to. A pale beetle stays pale its whole life. Just as wishing for wings will not make you grow feathers, an animal cannot will its own DNA to change.’
sentences: ‘No, Kwame, and that is a crucial point,’ said Madam Abena.
‘An individual organism cannot evolve or change its inherited colour simply because it needs or wishes to.
A pale beetle stays pale its whole life.
Just as wishing for wings will not make you grow feathers, an animal cannot will its own DNA to change.’
pages.alt: Madam Abena holds up one pale beetle model and shakes her head kindly to explain that an individual beetle cannot change its own shell colour.

pages.text: ‘Then how does the group change?’ asked Yaa. Madam Abena pointed to a diorama of hungry shrikes perched above dark soil. ‘On dark soil, birds easily spot the pale beetles and eat more of them. The beetles that happened to be born with darker shells blend in better. More of them survive long enough to lay eggs and pass their dark-shell genes to their offspring.’
sentences: ‘Then how does the group change?’ asked Yaa.
Madam Abena pointed to a diorama of hungry shrikes perched above dark soil.
‘On dark soil, birds easily spot the pale beetles and eat more of them.
The beetles that happened to be born with darker shells blend in better.
More of them survive long enough to lay eggs and pass their dark-shell genes to their offspring.’
pages.alt: A museum diorama shows a bird spotting pale beetles on dark soil while darker brown beetles remain hidden.

pages.text: ‘Over many generations,’ Madam Abena continued, ‘most beetles in the population have dark shells. We call a helpful inherited trait like that camouflage an adaptation, and the process that shifts the population over generations is called natural selection.’
sentences: ‘Over many generations,’ Madam Abena continued, ‘most beetles in the population have dark shells.
We call a helpful inherited trait like that camouflage an adaptation, and the process that shifts the population over generations is called natural selection.’
pages.alt: Yaa sketches two generations of beetles in her pad, showing dark-shelled beetles becoming more common over time.

pages.text: ‘We even see natural selection happening rapidly today,’ said Madam Abena. ‘When a person takes antibiotic medicine, most bacteria die, but a few bacteria with a rare inherited resistance trait may survive and multiply. That is why doctors tell us to finish our prescribed medicine properly.’
sentences: ‘We even see natural selection happening rapidly today,’ said Madam Abena.
‘When a person takes antibiotic medicine, most bacteria die, but a few bacteria with a rare inherited resistance trait may survive and multiply.
That is why doctors tell us to finish our prescribed medicine properly.’
pages.alt: A backlit science panel shows microscopic bacteria where a few resistant cells survive and multiply.

pages.text: They walked to a large branching tree diagram showing vertebrates, fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Kwame pointed to the primate branch. ‘Madam Abena, some people say evolution claims humans came from the monkeys we see in trees today. Is that true?’
sentences: They walked to a large branching tree diagram showing vertebrates, fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
Kwame pointed to the primate branch.
‘Madam Abena, some people say evolution claims humans came from the monkeys we see in trees today.
Is that true?’
pages.alt: Kwame points to a large illuminated branching tree of life on the museum wall.

pages.text: ‘Not at all,’ said Madam Abena. ‘Humans did not descend from today’s monkeys or modern apes. Think of your own family: you did not descend from your cousin! Instead, you and your cousin share grandparents. In a similar way, humans and modern apes are evolutionary cousins who share distant common ancestors that lived in Africa millions of years ago.’
sentences: ‘Not at all,’ said Madam Abena.
‘Humans did not descend from today’s monkeys or modern apes.
Think of your own family: you did not descend from your cousin!
Instead, you and your cousin share grandparents.
In a similar way, humans and modern apes are evolutionary cousins who share distant common ancestors that lived in Africa millions of years ago.’
pages.alt: Madam Abena traces two separate branches splitting from a lower trunk on the tree-of-life mural, showing cousins sharing an ancestor.

pages.text: ‘Why do scientists call it the theory of evolution if there is so much evidence?’ Yaa asked. ‘In everyday speech,’ said Madam Abena, ‘people use the word theory to mean a guess. But in science, a theory is the opposite of a guess. It is a comprehensive, well-tested explanation supported by many independent lines of evidence, from fossils and anatomy to DNA.’
sentences: ‘Why do scientists call it the theory of evolution if there is so much evidence?’ Yaa asked.
‘In everyday speech,’ said Madam Abena, ‘people use the word theory to mean a guess.
But in science, a theory is the opposite of a guess.
It is a comprehensive, well-tested explanation supported by many independent lines of evidence, from fossils and anatomy to DNA.’
pages.alt: A display case shows three matching lines of evidence side by side: a fossil bone, comparative limb bones, and a double-helix DNA model.

pages.text: Outside in the afternoon sunshine, Yaa looked at a weaver bird building its nest in a neem tree. Every feather, every leaf and every living creature carried a story written across millions of generations. ‘Life is always changing across generations,’ Yaa said, smiling at Kwame, ‘and evidence is how we read its history.’ The end.

pages.alt: Outside the museum in the sunshine, Yaa, Kwame and Madam Abena watch yellow weaver birds building nests in a green neem tree.

activities.question: What do fossils in deeper and higher rock layers show scientists?
options: A timeline of how living things have changed over millions of years
That every species alive today existed at the exact same time
That rocks grow like living plants
activities.explanation: Deeper rock layers preserve older organisms and higher layers preserve younger ones, recording change over geological time.

activities.question: Can an individual pale beetle change its shell colour to dark brown just because it needs to hide?
options: No; individuals do not evolve by wishing, populations shift over generations
Yes; any beetle can change its DNA whenever it feels scared
Yes; all insects change species every dry season
activities.explanation: Individual organisms cannot alter their inherited traits at will; natural selection acts on existing inherited variation across generations.

activities.definition: An inherited trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
distractors: A rock layer found at the bottom of the sea
A guess made without checking any evidence

activities.question: How does evolutionary science explain the relationship between humans and modern apes?
options: Humans and modern apes share distant common ancestors, like cousins
Humans descended from the monkeys living in zoos today
Humans and other mammals have no shared traits or DNA at all
activities.explanation: Humans did not descend from living monkeys or modern apes; rather, both lineages branched from common ancestors millions of years ago.

activities.question: What does the word "theory" mean in science?
options: A well-tested explanation supported by many independent lines of evidence
A random guess that has never been tested
A rule that can never be checked with observations
activities.explanation: In science, a theory (like germ theory, atomic theory, or evolutionary theory) is a rigorously tested explanation backed by converging evidence.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of natural selection in the beetle population in order.
items: Beetles in a population are born with inherited variation in shell colour.
Birds spot and eat more of the pale beetles on dark soil.
More dark-shelled beetles survive and lay eggs.
Over many generations, dark-shelled beetles become much more common.

activities.prompt: When you hear a common myth about science, how can you respond respectfully using evidence?

glossary.definition: Preserved remains or traces of ancient living things found in rock.
Natural differences in traits among individuals of the same species.
The young or children produced by living things.
An inherited trait that helps a living thing survive and reproduce in its environment.
Earlier generations from which later living things descended.
In science, a well-tested explanation supported by many lines of evidence.
